name: GW Orionis
description: Young triple star inside an ALMA-resolved disc broken into misaligned rings.

radius.source: Model radius derived from Kraus et al. (2020), Table S3: L = 48 solar luminosities and T = 5500 K; R/Rsun = sqrt(48) (5772/5500)^2, using the IAU nominal solar temperature. The luminosity is the unresolved light of three stars, so this is the sphere that would give that light, not a measured stellar radius

mass.source: Kraus et al. (2020), Table S5: total dynamical mass of the three stars, 5.26 +/- 0.22 solar masses, from their astrometric and radial-velocity orbits

temperature.source: Kraus et al. (2020), Table S3: adopted effective temperature

radialVelocity.source: Kraus et al. (2020), Table S5: velocity of the system's centre of mass, +27.96 +/- 0.12 km/s

distance.source: Kraus et al. (2020), Table S3: adopted distance, 388 +/- 5 pc, the one the paper's ring radii in astronomical units assume

limb.none: The sphere stands for the unresolved light of three stars. No resolved photosphere or applicable measured limb law is claimed.

text.card: A triple star whose planet-forming disc is broken into rings that lie in different planes.
text.introduction: ALMA resolves three dust rings around the three stars of GW Orionis. The innermost ring is tilted out of the plane of the outer two.
text.locator: Kraus et al. (2020), abstract and Table S6

notes: The three stars are drawn as one sphere: they lie 1.2 and 8.9 astronomical units apart, and their orbits are not drawn.
The disc's millimeter emission is observed; its third dimension is a reconstruction on the published ring planes.
The warped surface the paper models between the middle and inner rings from scattered light is not drawn.
